pages.text: The $(item)Optical Workshop$() turns blanks into optics. A lens's power is set by its two surfaces: $(thing)P = (n − 1)(C₁ − C₂)$(), with C the curvature of each - one over its radius. A 1-dioptre lens focuses at a metre.

Polishing wears the surface error down. Below a quarter of a wavelength the image is as sharp as diffraction allows; a Schmidt corrector needs an eighth, a grating a sixteenth. Longer polishing is truer, and slower.

Fused silica becomes lenses, $(item)Schmidt Corrector Plates$() and $(item)Echelle Gratings$(). Crystals need a Laue Pattern: fluorite lenses, moissanite lenses (its index, 2.65, makes a strong lens thin) and $(item)Sapphire Windows$(), four from a boule. Fluorite between two silica lenses is an $(item)Apochromatic Objective$().
Lithography lenses are really fluorite and fused silica: the workshop makes a $(item)Photonic Lens$() from them too.
